soil-agri-073.title: Terraces: staircases carved into hillsides
soil-agri-073.text: On steep ground, farmers have long cut the slope into a staircase. Each step is a terrace, a flat surface carved into a hill or mountainside for growing crops. Terraced fields reduce both erosion and surface runoff, and they can hold irrigated crops such as rice. Terracing is more common on small farms. Terraced paddies carry rice, wheat and barley across much of Asia, the Mediterranean Basin, Africa and South America. Terrace farming in the Levant goes back as early as the 4th millennium BCE. Terraces in the Yemen Highlands date from the start of the Bronze Age, in the 3rd millennium BC. In the Andes, the Wari and others built terraces called andenes before 1000 AD, to use shallow soil efficiently and irrigate crops; the Inca later adopted them. Dates from the method covered in {{ref:soil-hist-124}} show a major burst of Mediterranean terrace building in the later Middle Ages, around AD 1100–1600. Some dates remain unsettled. Scholars disagree on when the terraces of the Jerusalem Mountains were built, from the Bronze Age to the Roman and Byzantine periods. Such dates there may reflect later modification. Long-term moisture management by terracing can even create anthraquic Anthrosols.

soil-agri-091.title: Pedometric mapping turns soil into continuous grids
soil-agri-091.text: A traditional surveyor infers soil bodies from a mental model and draws them by hand. The result is subjective and hard to test for accuracy without extra sampling. Pedometric mapping, also called statistical soil mapping, produces soil property and soil class maps from data by statistical methods. It works largely through the statistics of data spread across space, the subject of {{ref:soil-meth-001}}. It predicts soil variables at unsampled places and estimates the uncertainty of each prediction. Its outputs come from rigorous statistical computing, so they are reproducible. Traditional mapping shows soil types as discrete bodies on polygon maps. Pedometric mapping shows measured properties as continuous grids, with maps of prediction error. Unlike {{ref:soil-agri-089}} as a whole, it relies strictly on these statistics and draws no discrete soil types. It leans on detailed covariate layers, maps of other variables such as elevation-model derivatives, remote sensing imagery, climate, land cover and geology. The aim is practical: predicting how a soil-plant ecosystem will respond to management.

soil-bio-003.title: Seven hundred kilometers of fungal thread in a gram of soil
soil-bio-003.text: A gram of garden soil can hold around one million fungi and around 700 km of fungal threads, called hyphae. Soil fungi are the yeasts, molds and other fungi of the soil. They lack chlorophyll, spread through the soil as a web of threads described in {{ref:soil-bio-217}}, and feed on dead plant and animal matter. Bacteria may outnumber them in cell counts, but fungi can contribute more biomass and respiration in some soils. As chemo-heterotrophs, they need organic substrates for their carbon. These threads break fresh remains down into {{ref:soil-bio-089}} and carbon dioxide. In that work the key fungi are {{ref:soil-bio-125}}, which turn dead matter into mineral forms such as nitrate, ammonium and phosphate that plants can use. Dead matter is colonized by a succession of species: sugar and starch users first, then those able to break down cellulose and tougher woody compounds. Many fungi are parasites that cause plant disease. Others are beneficial partners, such as {{ref:soil-bio-157}}, and fungi also help bind soil into crumbs and feed larger soil organisms. Compared with bacteria, fungi fare relatively well in acidic soils and in dry soils, which hold more of the oxygen they need. Fruiting bodies such as mushrooms release spores that spread by wind, water and fungus-eating animals and can lie dormant for years.

soil-bio-012.title: Actinomycetes, the bacteria once mistaken for fungi
soil-bio-012.text: The sweet, earthy smell of healthy soil comes from the volatile compounds of actinomycetes. These are soil bacteria of the phylum Actinomycetota, formerly Actinobacteria. They are Gram-positive and rich in guanine and cytosine, and many grow branching, fungus-like threads called mycelia. The order name Actinomycetales recalls that they were long thought to be fungi. Fungi do similar work, but actinomycetes are much smaller and likely fill a different niche. They decompose the remains of dead organisms so plants can take up the nutrients anew. They also help build stable dark soil matter by breaking down cellulose, tough woody compounds and the chitin of arthropods. The phylum is one of the dominant bacterial groups and includes {{ref:soil-bio-225}}, one of the largest bacterial genera. This genus and its relatives are major contributors to the biological buffering of soils. Some, such as {{ref:soil-bio-200}}, live with plant roots, fixing nitrogen in exchange for some of the plant's sugars. They need plenty of air and a pH between 6.0 and 7.5, but tolerate dry conditions better than most bacteria and fungi. They also stock the medicine cabinet. They yield many antibiotics, among them streptomycin, neomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline, plus farm compounds such as insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and plant growth promoters.

soil-bio-025.title: The soil food web, a digestive system for the land
soil-bio-025.text: All soil organic matter passes through a living gut of sorts. The soil food web is the community of organisms living all or part of their lives in soil. It is seen as a network of feeding links that passes energy among them. A food chain follows one linear energy pathway; a food web shows all the potential pathways. Plants are the producers. Using sunlight, they make plant material from carbon dioxide and minerals, and their roots exude acids, sugars and enzymes that feed the web underground. Its members range from bacteria, algae, fungi and protozoa to {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, and on to earthworms, insects and small vertebrates. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break dead plant and animal material into simple nutrients. In this way the web processes dead material much as a digestive system processes food. The work reaches beyond the soil. The web keeps manure, plant residues and pesticides out of water, holds nitrogen back from groundwater, fixes nitrogen and helps water soak in. Its members prey on crop pests and feed animals above ground. Once thought simple, soil food webs turned out to have common omnivory and long, complex chains. Those chains still resist drying, freezing and fumigation. Some influence escapes the diagram, though. Litter transformers, mutualists and {{ref:soil-bio-004}} strongly affect their communities in ways food webs do not capture.

soil-bio-055.title: The enzymatic latch that holds decay in check
soil-bio-055.text: In {{ref:soil-class-070}}, one family of enzymes holds the key to decay. The enzymatic latch is the control of breakdown in this waterlogged material by phenol oxidases. Phenolic compounds inhibit the hydrolase enzymes that digest dead material. Phenol oxidases destroy those phenolics and so release decay, which means limits on the microbes limit breakdown. Saprotrophic bacteria release microbial extracellular enzymes (MEEs) when their energy and nutrient needs are unmet, so MEEs signal nutrient availability. Several tell a story. One, {{ref:soil-bio-257}}, releases sugars that give microbes energy and easily used carbon. Acid and alkaline phosphatases show the potential to free phosphorus from organic forms. Phenol oxidases can also degrade or detoxify aromatic pollutants into carbon sources.

soil-bio-070.title: Microbial inoculants: bottled helpers for crops
soil-bio-070.text: An estimated 836 million USD is spent on microbial inoculants each year. These farm amendments, also called soil inoculants or bioinoculants, use beneficial microbes that live around or inside roots to promote plant health. Many of the microbes form mutually beneficial partnerships with the crop. Besides improving nutrition, they can promote growth by stimulating the plant's hormone production. Bacterial inoculants, called plant growth promoting {{ref:soil-bio-154}}, include nitrogen fixers and phosphate solubilisers. The most commonly applied is {{ref:soil-bio-239}}, which fixes nitrogen inside legume roots, in the growths covered in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are used to supply phosphorus. In one greenhouse with reduced fertilization, these fungi plus root bacteria gave tomato yields at 70% fertility that matched those at 100%. Inoculants can also induce systemic acquired resistance, a whole-plant defense, shown so far against powdery mildew, take-all, leaf spot and root rot. Mixing strains raises nutrient uptake from soil and fertilizer. Several strains together even raise the activity of the nitrogen-fixing enzyme when only one of them fixes nitrogen. Inoculants often change the soil's existing microbial community. Results so far are mixed. Research in 2024 suggests as few as one in nine commercial products are beneficial, and with commercial products root colonization by these fungi was under 10%. Large-scale application is not yet economically viable, so inoculants are not widely used in industrial agriculture.

soil-bio-091.title: What humus is made of, and why it is hard to say
soil-bio-091.text: Chemists in the 1940s and 1960s tried to take humus apart, and they failed. Their extractants reacted with the organic matter and created artifacts. Humus remains a very complex substance that is still not fully understood. Its core is very large molecules, built partly from lignin and other plant polyphenols and partly from similar molecules made by microbes. Proteins, amino acids and {{ref:soil-bio-260}} attach to this base, giving humus a moderate nitrogen and sulfur content. The method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}} shows the base, mostly lignin and black carbon, can be very old, while the attachments are much younger. Microbes strip the protein more readily than they break the base, and younger protein may take its place. In the classical view of {{ref:soil-hist-018}}, fully humified humus is amorphous, uniformly dark, spongy and jelly-like. Yet under a light microscope it may still show tiny plant, animal and microbial remains, broken up mechanically but not chemically.

soil-bio-136.title: How roots feel their way through the soil
soil-bio-136.text: Roots are not blind diggers. They sense gravity, light, physical barriers and soil conditions, and they steer their growth in response. Gravitropism, growth guided by gravity and worked through auxin, one of the {{ref:soil-bio-245}}, sends roots downward from germination. Each root type holds its own set angle. Air, nutrients and water pull roots toward them, and roots turn away from dry or otherwise poor soil. Roots hunting for nutrients can sense compacted soil through the diffusion of ethylene gas, and avoid it. They can even tell their own roots from other plants' roots in the same soil. Given years, roots crack foundations, snap water lines and lift sidewalks.

soil-bio-154.title: Rhizobacteria, the bacteria that live on roots
soil-bio-154.text: Not every bacterium on a root is a friend. Rhizobacteria are bacteria that live with plant roots and can harm plant growth, leave it alone or help it. In practice the word usually means the helpful ones, described in {{ref:soil-bio-155}}; they make up about 2–5% of rhizosphere bacteria. Some colonize the root surface or the spaces between outer root cells, often forming nodules. Others live inside the plant, in the apoplast, the spaces outside its cells, the subject of {{ref:soil-bio-202}}. One of their most useful acts is turning N2 gas, which plants cannot use, into ammonia the host can take up. That service is costly. Building and keeping nodules can take 12–25% of a plant's total photosynthetic output. Rhizobacteria also release organic acids and phosphatases that turn insoluble soil phosphorus into usable forms such as H2PO4−. Free-living nitrogen fixers live just outside the roots of many grasses. In rice they supply more fixed nitrogen when the plant's demand is high. Organic amendments such as sugarcane straw, goat manure and filter mud boost these free-living helpers, even without nodules.

soil-bio-179.title: Root nodules, the pink factories of fixed nitrogen
soil-bio-179.text: Cut open a working nodule and its fixing zone is pink, colored by an iron-containing protein that manages oxygen, {{ref:soil-fert-219}}. A root nodule is a growth on the roots of some plants, chiefly legumes, that houses nitrogen-fixing bacteria: rhizobia in legumes, or {{ref:soil-bio-200}} in other plants. Fixation is very sensitive to oxygen. Nodules form when soil nitrogen is scarce; plenty of it blocks them. Legume roots release flavonoids that attract rhizobia and switch on {{ref:soil-bio-201}}. These make root hairs curl, and an infection thread carries the bacteria into the cortex. Leaf sugars pay for splitting N2. Determinate nodules, as on soybean, stop dividing early and are round. Indeterminate ones, as on pea, alfalfa and clover, keep a growing tip and are cylindrical. Heat, acidic soils, drought and nitrate limit it. When the plant dies, its fixed nitrogen fertilizes the soil, which is why traditional rotations include a legume such as clover.

soil-chem-077.title: What becomes of a pollutant once it reaches soil
soil-chem-077.text: A chemical spilled on soil does not simply sit there. Environmental soil chemistry studies how contaminants are released into soil and what becomes of them. Processes such as {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, {{ref:soil-chem-147}}, precipitation, polymerization, dissolution, hydrolysis, hydration, complexation and oxidation–reduction can each raise or lower a chemical's toxicity. Knowing these reactions helps predict a contaminant's fate and design sound, cost-effective clean-up, though clean-up engineers often disregard them. The field grew from worry, since the late 1960s, about pollution and its ecological and health risks.

soil-chem-091.title: Smectite, the swelling clay with an open interior
soil-chem-091.text: Smectite clays swell because their layers are not rigidly joined. Smectite is a group of swelling 2:1 clay minerals, chiefly {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, that take water and cations between their layers. The name depends on place: smectite is the usual term in Europe, while North America uses the name of its chief member, and industry calls these clays {{ref:soil-chem-100}}. Each layer is two silica tetrahedral sheets cross-linked through an octahedral sheet of alumina or iron oxide. Isomorphous substitution in both kinds of sheet gives the layers their negative charge. The interlayer between them holds hydrated cations and water. These enter reversibly, so the clay swells as they come in. That open interlayer also gives smectites the highest {{ref:soil-chem-046}} of the clays common in soils; only vermiculite and some zeolites exceed it. Smectites form by weathering of basalt, gabbro and silica-rich volcanic glass, and where hot water or seawater dissolves much of the silica from volcanic ash. Soils with smectite clay expand when wet. Clay soils containing smectite also suffer more problems from {{ref:soil-chem-142}} than illite or kaolinite clay soils.

soil-chem-111.title: Ferrihydrite, iron oxide as a nanoparticle sponge
soil-chem-111.text: A single gram of ferrihydrite offers several hundred square metres of surface. This widespread, poorly crystalline hydrous iron(III) oxyhydroxide exists only as fine-grained nanoparticles. It forms in soils, waters, aquifers and mining areas, precipitating from oxygenated iron-rich water or through bacterial activity. Its nanoporous particles adsorb arsenic, lead, phosphate and the organic acids met in {{ref:soil-chem-059}} and {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Ferrihydrite is metastable, a precursor of hematite and goethite, though adsorbed impurities such as silica usually block that change in nature. Under reducing conditions, as in gley soils and often with microbial help, it can turn into {{ref:soil-chem-170}}, here in the form covered in {{ref:soil-chem-109}}. Brief contact with air oxidizes it back to ferrihydrite.

soil-chem-115.title: Reducing agents, the electron givers
soil-chem-115.text: In soil, the main giver of electrons is soil organic matter. A reducing agent reduces another substance by giving it electrons, and is itself oxidized. It is also called a reductant, the role taken up in {{ref:soil-chem-177}}. Electropositive metals such as lithium, sodium, magnesium, iron, zinc and aluminium give up electrons readily, which makes them good reducing agents. Underground, donors include that same material, hydrogen, methane, reduced sulfur and iron compounds, and ammonium. Biochemists speak of a reducing equivalent: whatever transfers the equivalent of one electron, whether an electron or a hydrogen atom.

soil-chem-129.title: Methanogenesis: the last step of decay without air
soil-chem-129.text: Methane has 25 times the global warming potential of carbon dioxide, averaged over 100 years, and wet soils make a lot of it. Methanogenesis is the making of methane by the microbes in {{ref:soil-chem-174}}, all of them archaea, as the final step in breaking down dead plant and animal material without oxygen. It sits at the bottom of {{ref:soil-chem-122}}. Once every electron acceptor except carbon dioxide is spent, only methanogenesis and fermentation can proceed. Without it, much carbon would pile up as fermentation products. In most freshwater wetlands sulfate is scarce, and methanogenesis takes over only once sulfate is used up. In sediments, sulfate reducers take most of the hydrogen in upper layers, while the methane makers dominate lower down. In the oxygen-free layers of {{ref:soil-class-070}}, they combine carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas into methane and water. Production runs high in flooded rice fields, wetlands, and anoxic floodplain, lake and reservoir sediments. Other microbes, {{ref:soil-env-280}}, oxidize methane back to carbon dioxide. Aerating such soils raises sulfate and nitrate, which cut methane output. In upland soils, methanogenesis is often confined to anoxic microsites inside otherwise aerobic soil.

soil-class-086.title: Calcareous grassland, the grazed turf of chalk downs
soil-class-086.text: Calcareous grassland, also called alkaline grassland, grows on thin, basic soils such as those of chalk and limestone downland, where shallow soils like {{ref:soil-class-050}} are common. Large areas occur in northwestern Europe, especially on Salisbury Plain and the North and South Downs of England. One variant on calcium-rich shell sand is {{ref:soil-class-158}}. Short, hardy grasses and herbs such as clover dominate, held at a plagioclimax, a stage fixed by sheep or cattle grazing. It is an important habitat for insects, particularly butterflies and ants. Its lichens, favored by stable flints and nutrient-poor soil, have declined since the mid-20th century through reduced grazing, nitrogen settling from the air and habitat loss.

soil-env-012.title: Soil remediation: dig it up, treat it or wall it in
soil-env-012.text: Before contaminated land is redeveloped, it may first have to be cleaned. Soil remediation is that cleanup: removing, treating or containing pollutants to restore the soil's functions and values. Planning starts with field measurements of soil chemicals and with computer models of how those chemicals move and change. Every method falls on one side of a line. Ex situ methods excavate soil or pump groundwater for treatment at the surface. In situ methods treat the contamination where it lies. The traditional approaches are digging soil out for landfill and pumping out and treating groundwater, as in {{ref:soil-env-250}}. Excavation even extends to dredging contaminated bay muds and canals. Physical options include aerating soil on site, at the risk of air pollution, or heating it so contaminants turn to vapor and can be drawn off. Living things offer another route. Microbes, plants such as willow and fungi can break contaminants down or take up toxic metals, as {{ref:soil-env-023}} explains. Other in situ tools include solidifying and stabilizing the soil, reactive barriers that treat passing groundwater, chemical oxidation, and heating in place. Sometimes the answer is to leave the pollution and contain it. Barrier walls such as slurry walls must be impermeable and resist attack by the waste for their whole lifespan. Cleanup follows regulations. Where no standards exist, or they are only advisory, it rests on assessments of health and ecological risk.

soil-env-026.title: Natural attenuation: letting a site clean itself, under watch
soil-env-026.text: Sometimes the best cleanup crew is already in the ground. Natural attenuation is the breakdown of contaminants by a site's own microbes, with no human intervention, though the site must still be monitored. It is one of the broad categories of bioremediation, beside feeding the native microbes and adding new ones. Time helps in other ways too. Contaminants can become less bioavailable, harder for living things to take up, while microbes and whole ecosystems adapt to them. Monitored natural attenuation is one technique for remediating derelict soils, alongside leaching, {{ref:soil-env-240}}, soil conditioners, phytoremediation and other bioremediation. Stepping in can even backfire. Where reducing conditions favor anaerobic bacteria, injecting oxygen to speed aerobic attenuation can suppress the anaerobic kind.

soil-env-154.title: Carbon in the deep freeze: the permafrost carbon cycle
soil-env-154.text: Permafrost-affected soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land, yet they store between 25 and 50% of its soil organic carbon. The permafrost carbon cycle is the Arctic part of the global carbon cycle. Carbon moves from frozen soils to plants, microbes and the air. It returns to permafrost through burial and sedimentation driven by freezing, or cryogenic, processes, while some passes to the ocean and the wider cycle. The cycle includes exchanges of carbon dioxide and methane with the air. It also includes transfers to water as dissolved and particulate carbon, both organic and inorganic. Because permafrost responds slowly to climate, it keeps carbon out of the air for long periods. The method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}} shows much of it is thousands of years old. Early carbon estimates and climate models often neglected this reservoir, but research on it has grown enormously since the 2000s. Microbial respiration is the main route by which old permafrost carbon re-enters the air. Soil temperature, moisture, nutrients and oxygen set its rate. Minerals can slow the escape. Iron oxides can hold back respiration, and iron and aluminum can adsorb freed carbon, especially in the sandy layers often found over permafrost. Despite the huge stores, the whole pool is unlikely to mobilize, because much permafrost will stay frozen even as thaw deepens.

soil-fert-008.title: Phosphate fertilizers, from rock to soluble salt
soil-fert-008.text: Each ton of phosphoric acid made from phosphate rock leaves five tons of an impure radioactive waste, {{ref:soil-fert-213}}. The world produces 100 to 280 million tons of it a year. That waste is the shadow of phosphate fertilizers, which supply phosphorus from rock whose main minerals are fluorapatite and hydroxyapatite. Acid treatment turns those minerals into water-soluble phosphate salts, and this use is the main reason so much sulfuric acid is made. The main straight phosphate fertilizers are the acid-treated rock products of {{ref:soil-fert-094}}. The single kind has 14–18% P2O5 plus this waste; the triple kind has 44–48% P2O5 and no gypsum. A maize crop yielding 6–9 tonnes of grain per hectare needs 31–50 kg of phosphate fertilizer, and soybeans about half, 20–25 kg. Billions of kilograms of rock are mined each year, but the remaining ore is shrinking in size and quality, making future supply a critical issue. Phosphate also pollutes. Normally a limiting nutrient in water, at high concentrations it promotes cyanobacteria and algae, and it is the main contributor to {{ref:soil-env-020}}.

soil-fert-042.title: Closing the loop: human excreta as fertilizer
soil-fert-042.text: In Africa, the nutrients theoretically recoverable from human excreta match all current fertilizer use. That makes excreta a possible alternative for smallholders, who often cannot afford chemical fertilizer. Reusing treated excreta for its nutrients, organic matter and energy 'closes the loop' between sanitation and farming, and it is central to {{ref:soil-fert-207}}. The products differ: urine, dried feces, composted feces, fecal sludge, sewage and sewage sludge each fertilize in their own way. Treatments such as urine diversion and drying, composting, and sludge treatment remove pathogens to varying degrees and cut water content. The advantages are real. Fertilizers made from mined phosphate rock can carry cadmium and uranium into the food chain, but excreta-based ones generally lack these heavy metals. Their nutrients are bound in organic compounds or held on humic acids, so they release slowly and leach less readily than mineral fertilizers. Like other nitrogen fertilizers, though, they can let nitrate leach away. Pharmaceutical residues in excreta break down better in soil than in water. People have farmed with excreta for centuries, often in unregulated and unsafe ways in developing countries. Whether reuse is cost-effective is still debated.

soil-fert-113.title: Nitrifying bacteria, a crew that works in two shifts
soil-fert-113.text: Nitrifying bacteria work in two shifts. They are chemolithotrophs, microbes that live by oxidizing inorganic chemicals, as {{ref:soil-bio-057}} explains; these ones oxidize ammonia or nitrite. Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria make nitrite, and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria turn it into nitrate, so the two groups grow together. In soil, the first group converts ammonia from decomposing organic matter or fertilizer, and the second uses the nitrite. Soil genera include Nitrosospira, an ammonia oxidizer, and the nitrite oxidizers {{ref:soil-fert-221}} and the genus in {{ref:soil-fert-147}}. Key enzymes sit on their internal membranes: ammonia monooxygenase, hydroxylamine oxidoreductase and nitrite oxidoreductase. They are most numerous where ammonia is plentiful, such as sites of heavy protein decomposition and sewage treatment plants. Winogradsky described the two-step process in 1890.

soil-fert-159.title: Iron, the metal behind green leaves
soil-fert-159.text: Iron is not part of chlorophyll, yet a plant cannot make chlorophyll without it. This micronutrient is an enzyme cofactor, a helper the enzymes need, in photosynthesis and electron transport. Deficiency yellows the tissue between the veins, a form of {{ref:soil-fert-228}}, and causes necrosis. It can stem from excess heavy metals or lime in the soil, or from a lack of copper. Iron(II) is the most useful form because it is more soluble at neutral pH. Plants can also use iron(III) through the photo-reduction of ferric citrate. In the field, iron fertilizer is supplied as a chelate, a compound that holds the metal in a form plants can take up.

soil-fert-188.title: Grid sampling: mapping a field's nutrients square by square
soil-fert-188.text: Nutrients are rarely spread evenly across a field. Grid soil sampling collects GPS-located samples on a regular grid to estimate how they vary. The distribution and resolution of the samples are chosen to capture how the field varies from spot to spot, the subject of {{ref:soil-meth-005}}, weighing the goals of the analysis against the cost of sampling. In U.S. corn and soybean regions, many providers offer one sample per 2.5-acre grid. A reference map recording sample locations and quantities is needed to interpret the results.

soil-form-018.title: Epipedons, the diagnostic surface horizons of USDA taxonomy
soil-form-018.text: {{ref:soil-class-006}} gives the top of the soil its own set of names. An epipedon is a diagnostic surface horizon, the upper part of the soil. There are eight: the anthropic, folistic, histic, melanic, mollic, ochric, plaggen and umbric epipedons. {{ref:soil-form-118}}, fertile and built by long additions of root-derived organic material, is the defining feature of {{ref:soil-class-101}}. {{ref:soil-class-098}} must have a histic epipedon, while an ochric epipedon is common in {{ref:soil-class-094}} and {{ref:soil-class-093}}. {{ref:soil-class-100}} usually have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon. Plaggen or anthropic epipedons signal intense, prolonged human activity.

soil-form-030.title: Umbric horizons, dark but acid
soil-form-030.text: Shade is in the name: umbric comes from the Latin umbra. An umbric horizon is a thick, dark, organic-rich surface horizon that is acid and low in bases. It normally has a pH below 5.5 and a {{ref:soil-chem-052}} under 50 percent. WRB criteria include Munsell chroma and value of 3 or less when moist, and at least 0.6% organic carbon. It must be at least 100 mm thick on hard rock, otherwise 200 mm. Roots growing horizontally can indicate its acidity. Similar dark, base-poor layers made by deep cultivation, manuring or the kitchen refuse heaps in {{ref:soil-hist-102}} are told apart by artifacts, spade marks or land-use history.

soil-form-042.title: How bare rock slowly becomes living soil
soil-form-042.text: In the Mediterranean climate of Sicily, weathering makes new soil at roughly 1/10 mm a year. That slow work is soil formation, also called pedogenesis: the development of soil as shaped by place, environment and history. It begins with the {{ref:soil-found-052}} of freshly accumulated parent material. New soils then deepen through further weathering and through deposition, including settling dust. Microbes feed on the nutrients that weathering releases. They produce organic acids and proteins that speed the breakdown of minerals, and their residues help build the dark, decayed organic matter of the topsoil. As the soil develops, pioneer species arrive first, then richer plant and animal communities through {{ref:soil-form-125}}. Topsoil deepens as remains of dead plants and microbes accumulate and mix with weathered minerals. With maturity come layers. Accumulating organic matter, mineral weathering and the washing of dissolved material downward create horizons that differ in color, structure, texture and chemistry. Biogeochemical processes both build and destroy order within a soil. Differences in the conditions that shape soils produce patterns in where soil types occur. Pedogenesis is studied as a branch of pedology. It explains how soils are spread across the land today and how they were spread in past geological periods.

soil-form-066.title: Laterization: rain, drought and millions of years
soil-form-066.text: Laterization was most active from the mid-Tertiary to the mid-Quaternary, 35 to 1.5 million years ago, and it has not stopped. It is the prolonged chemical weathering of rock under tropical conditions that produces laterite. It needs high temperatures and heavy rainfall alternating with dry seasons. Rain leaches the rock, and in the dry season capillary action lifts the dissolved ions to the surface. Acid dissolves the host minerals. Hydrolysis precipitates insoluble iron and aluminum oxides, while sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium are leached away. Solutions of the right pH dissolve silica in preference to the iron and aluminum oxides, leaving mainly those two metals behind. The first products are weathered rocks called saprolites, and quartz is the most abundant mineral surviving from the parent rock. Gentle crests and plateaus help by protecting the weathered cover from erosion. The parent rock shapes the result. Mafic, iron-rich rocks yield {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, granitic iron-poor rocks yield aluminum ores, and ultramafic rocks yield nickel laterites. The process slowed with abrupt global cooling and continues today at a reduced rate.

soil-form-089.title: Transported parent material, soil from somewhere else
soil-form-089.text: Most soils form in material that wind, water, ice and gravity have carried many miles. Transported parent material is loose, uncemented material moved this way, and it is named for its last means of transport. Material a glacier carried and streams then redeposited counts as stream-transported, or glacial fluvial, parent material. The recognized carriers are wind, water, gravity, ice, lakes and oceans, and the entries ahead give each deposit its name. Water-carried material is split three ways: by rivers, in lakes or in the sea. Wind sorts its load. It moves silt and fine sand hundreds of miles to build {{ref:soil-form-106}}. It seldom moves clay, which sticks into stable clumps. Wind also piles sand-sized grains into dunes and drops {{ref:soil-form-152}} at various distances from a volcano. In the field, rock fragments that thin out with depth, especially over saprolite, suggest the soil material has moved downslope.

soil-form-101.title: Deep weathering, rock rotting for millions of years
soil-form-101.text: At 20 m per million years, weathering needs several million years to build a deep regolith, and cooler climates need longer. Deep weathering is that long-continued chemical attack. It builds thick, deeply weathered regolith over bedrock, the product of a region's long weathering history. Three conditions favor it. Relief must be gentle enough to prevent erosion and let water carry dissolved material down. The crust must stay tectonically stable for a long time. The climate must be humid, tropical to temperate, with warmth to speed the reactions. Deeply weathered profiles are widespread between latitudes 35°N and 35°S. In parts of Africa, India, South America, Australia and southeast Asia, regolith has been forming for over 100 million years. Regoliths range from a few metres to over 150 m thick, depending on surface age, tectonics, climate history and bedrock. The process sorts the elements as it goes. Sulfides and carbonates leave readily. Nickel, cobalt, copper and zinc held in iron- and magnesium-rich minerals stay higher. They reprecipitate with iron–manganese oxides in the middle and lower saprolite. The result is secondary and supergene ores, enriched near the surface by weathering: {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, iron ores, saprolitic gold, supergene copper, uranium and residual {{ref:soil-chem-193}}. Sweden shows the process across deep time. There it formed thin clay-rich saprolites 1,000 to 500 million years ago, thick ones 200 to 66 million years ago, and medium-thick immature ones 5 million years ago.

soil-form-112.title: Alluvium, the sediment that rivers leave behind
soil-form-112.text: Some of the earliest human civilizations grew on river mud. Alluvium is loose clay, silt, sand or gravel deposited by running water in stream beds, on floodplains, in {{ref:soil-water-293}} or similar settings. Floodplain alluvium can be highly fertile. It is usually geologically young and unconsolidated, and most of it is Quaternary. It is often called cover, because it hides the bedrock beneath. Running water sorts what it drops, so alluvium is generally fine-grained and well sorted. Seasonal floods leave it in layers on floodplains. The fans coarsen toward the uplands, and deltas at river mouths are fine-grained. Sediment laid down in seas, estuaries, lakes or ponds is not called alluvium. Beyond that, geologists still disagree over which other deposits the term should include. The word is old. Antoine Furetière's dictionary, published in 1690, defined alluvion as new land formed by sediment along rivers and seas. In the 19th century alluvium meant river sediment lying above older diluvium, which was ascribed to Noah's flood. Once that idea was rejected, diluvium became older alluvium.

soil-found-022.title: Soil life and pH, each shaping the other
soil-found-022.text: pH shapes soil life, and soil life shapes pH. Microbes and animals respond to pH directly and through nutrient status, {{ref:soil-env-257}} and the forms described in {{ref:soil-bio-095}}, so communities shift as pH changes. At low pH, aluminum causes oxidative stress that harms soft-bodied fauna without a hard outer skeleton: protists, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, {{ref:soil-bio-087}} and earthworms. The traffic runs both ways. Many fungi acidify soil by excreting oxalic acid, which locks calcium into insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Earthworm mucus, weakly alkaline at pH 7.5 to 8, buffers pH. Burrowing animals that mix organic and mineral matter reduce acidity, as in {{ref:soil-bio-096}}.

soil-found-032.title: Quartz and feldspar, the sturdy framework silicates
soil-found-032.text: Quartz is the most abundant mineral species, making up 12% of the crust. It belongs to the framework silicates, whose tetrahedra share all four corners. This is the most polymerized class. Strong covalent bonds make these minerals particularly stable chemically, and quartz is highly resistant. That toughness makes it a marker. A rock rich in quartz is considered mature, because quartz, one of the {{ref:soil-form-140}}, is the one that survived heavy weathering. The most abundant mineral group in the crust is the one described in {{ref:soil-form-141}}. In them, Al3+ takes the place of some Si4+, and added potassium, sodium or calcium balances the charge. These minerals matter to soil for another reason: their weathering is a common source of the fine minerals in {{ref:soil-found-040}}.

soil-found-040.title: Clay, the finest and busiest part of soil
soil-found-040.text: Some of the earliest pottery shards date to around 14,000 BCE, which makes clay the longest-known ceramic raw material. Clay is a fine-grained natural soil material containing {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, the hydrous aluminum sheet silicates described in {{ref:soil-found-033}}. In pure form these minerals are mostly white or pale. Impurities color natural clays, and small amounts of iron oxide give red or brown tones. Wet clay is plastic, and firing hardens it. In a field, clay is a mixed blessing. Clay soils drain poorly, which makes them generally less suited to crops. Yet they are more fertile, because they hold on to more positively charged nutrients. Soils rich in swelling clays, which expand as they absorb water, are a major challenge in civil engineering. Mix sand, silt and less than 40% clay, and the result is {{ref:soil-phys-012}}. Clay lasts in rock as well. Shale, formed largely from clay, is the most common {{ref:soil-form-136}}.

soil-found-054.title: Frost weathering and the ice that splits rock
soil-found-054.text: Water expands 9.2% when it freezes. Inside rock, the pressure this creates has a realistic upper limit of 14 megapascals, far above granite's tensile strength of about 4 megapascals. Frost weathering is physical weathering caused by ice forming inside rock outcrops. Frost wedging, the classic explanation, was long believed the main mechanism. It needs small, twisting cracks in almost saturated rock and daily freeze–thaw cycles. Those conditions are unusual, so it is unlikely to matter in the tropics, polar regions or arid climates. Growing theoretical and experimental work now favors {{ref:soil-phys-179}} instead, though the question is still open. Water drawn to the growing ice layers covered in {{ref:soil-phys-154}} can exert up to ten times the pressure of frost wedging. It works best between −4 and −15 °C.

soil-found-061.title: Oxidation weathering: iron that reddens and weakens rock
soil-found-061.text: A reddish-brown crust on a rock is often a sign of iron changing inside it. Oxidation weathering is chemical weathering by oxidation of metals in minerals, most commonly iron changing from Fe2+ to Fe3+. Oxygen and water drive the change. They turn Fe2+ into Fe3+ oxides and hydroxides such as {{ref:soil-chem-165}}. The new surface crumbles easily, and the rock beneath grows weaker. Sulfide minerals oxidize too. Chalcopyrite, for example, turns to copper hydroxide and {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, leaving colored deposits. The process reaches into the soil. Oxidizing {{ref:soil-form-140}}, especially sulfides and those containing Fe2+, generates soil acidity.

soil-found-077.title: Soil: rock, water, air and life in one mixture
soil-found-077.text: A single gram of soil can hold billions of organisms from thousands of species, most of them microbes that no one has yet explored. Soil is a natural mixture of minerals, {{ref:soil-bio-114}}, gases, water and organisms that together support the life of plants and soil creatures. All of Earth's soil, taken together, forms one layer with a name of its own, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-084}}. Soil is a three-state system. A solid framework of minerals and dead plant and animal material is laced with pores. Those pores hold gases, the soil atmosphere, and water carrying dissolved substances, {{ref:soil-found-079}}. Much of a soil is empty space. A dry sample of most soils weighs 1.1 to 1.6 grams per cubic centimeter, yet the particles themselves weigh 2.6 to 2.7. Soil is made by climate, relief, organisms and the rock or sediment beneath acting together over time, and it never stops developing. It is also young. Little of it is older than the Pleistocene and none is older than the Cenozoic, though fossilized soils survive from as far back as the Archean. Soil has four important functions. It grows plants, stores and purifies water, modifies Earth's atmosphere and houses soil organisms. It is a large reservoir of carbon, and possibly one of the most sensitive to human disturbance and climate change. Soil ecologists regard it as an ecosystem in its own right. Some scientific definitions keep the word dirt for soil that has been moved out of place.

soil-hist-041.title: The World Soil Museum, a gallery of soil profiles
soil-hist-041.text: In Wageningen, in the Netherlands, the world's major soil types stand side by side. The World Soil Museum displays soil profile monoliths, preserved vertical slices of real soil profiles. It is managed by {{ref:soil-hist-049}}, an independent science-based foundation. It began as the International Soil Museum, at the request of UNESCO and the International Society of Soil Science, to support the FAO-UNESCO map described in {{ref:soil-hist-117}}. Some 80 monoliths are on display. A much larger collection of some 1000, from over 70 countries, waits in its repository. Each comes with a horizon-by-horizon description and data. Visitors see examples of the 32 WRB Reference Soil Groups, a section on Dutch soils and soils much changed by long human use.

soil-phys-054.title: Two meanings of clay: a size and a mineral
soil-phys-054.text: The word clay hides two different ideas. One is a class of very fine particle sizes; the other is material made of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}. The two overlap but differ. The size boundary with silt depends on the discipline: 2 μm for soil scientists, 4–5 μm for many sedimentologists, 1 μm for chemists who study {{ref:soil-chem-154}}. Geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity rather than size, using {{ref:soil-phys-021}}. A clay-sized grain may be very fine quartz, sharing clay's surface-area traits but not its {{ref:soil-chem-047}}, the holding of nutrients.

soil-phys-089.title: What compaction does to roots, microbes and rivers
soil-phys-089.text: Grassland soil without traffic takes in water five times faster than severely trafficked soil. Compaction chiefly cuts how readily air and water enter the ground. Denser soil with smaller pores restricts roots, partly through build-up of the hormone ethylene, and limits their access to nutrients. Shallow roots can leave the topsoil extremely dry and cracked. Oxygen diffuses poorly, so soil can turn airless. With wetter conditions this boosts {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, raising N2O emissions and leaving less nitrogen for crops. Waterlogged compacted soils also release methane through increased bacterial activity. Severe compaction can shrink {{ref:soil-bio-269}} and, by removing large pores, shift where earthworms live. Wheel tracks often start runoff and erosion, carrying sediment, nutrients and pesticides off the field to over-enrich lakes and rivers. Less water reaches the groundwater, a serious risk in dry regions. Over large areas, the yield losses may threaten food security.

soil-phys-107.title: Cohesion: the strength that is not friction
soil-phys-107.text: Friction explains most of a soil's strength, but not all of it. Cohesion is the part of a soil's or rock's shear strength that does not depend on friction between particles. In soils it comes from electrostatic forces in stiff clays that once bore heavier loads, from cementing by Fe2O3, CaCO3 or NaCl, and from negative capillary pressure. The pore pressure response when water cannot drain adds some, and so do plant roots. Several sources are temporary. Weathering can remove electrostatic bonds, wetting removes capillary suction, time dissipates pore pressure, and logging or fire removes root strength. The theory in {{ref:soil-phys-169}} usually measures cohesion as the shear strength at zero normal pressure on the failure surface. Values run from 0 to 48 kPa for very soft clay, through 192 to 384 kPa for stiff clay, to 384 to 766 kPa for very stiff clay. When soil loses cohesion it can slough off banks and slopes.

soil-phys-125.title: Seepage: water on the move through soil
soil-phys-125.text: Still water in soil does little harm. Moving water can bring down a levee. Seepage is the movement of water through soil. Below the {{ref:soil-water-247}}, where pore water pressure rises evenly with depth, conditions are hydrostatic and nothing flows. A sloping or perched water surface sets water seeping. The rate follows {{ref:soil-water-201}}. Flow is proportional to how fast excess pressure changes with distance, scaled by how freely the soil passes water and by the fluid's viscosity. The ease of flow varies enormously, from about 10−12 m/s in clays to about 10−1 m/s in gravels. In steady seepage, velocities do not change with time; that does not hold while water levels are changing or the soil is consolidating. Upward seepage lowers effective stress. At the critical {{ref:soil-phys-166}}, it reaches zero, the soil loses nearly all strength, and less permeable layers may heave. This state, also called a boiling condition, is the one behind {{ref:soil-phys-116}} and {{ref:soil-phys-118}}. Strength lost to upward seepage often helps cause levee failures. Fast seepage also drags particles away from where it comes out. The erosion works back upslope as {{ref:soil-water-289}}, which can fail a structure and open sinkholes. To stop seepage below dams, engineers build impermeable curtains of {{ref:soil-chem-100}}, a clay almost fully saturated with sodium.

soil-phys-141.title: Quartz, water and air: how well soil conducts heat
soil-phys-141.text: Quartz conducts heat at 8.8 W·m−1·K−1; dry soil manages only 0.2–0.4. Soil thermal conductivity is the ability of soil to conduct heat. In the same units, typical values are 0.57 for water, 0.25 for {{ref:soil-bio-114}} and 1–3 for wet soil. Air conducts heat poorly and weakens conduction through the solid and liquid parts. The solid phase conducts best, yet the varying moisture of a soil largely decides its conductivity. Designing a shallow-loop heat pump that draws on the ground, as in {{ref:soil-phys-178}}, needs an accurate on-site reading, which a thermal heat probe can provide.

soil-phys-165.title: Hydraulic head, the height that tells groundwater where to go
soil-phys-165.text: What moves groundwater is not height alone, but height plus pressure. Hydraulic head is a liquid's pressure, divided by its {{ref:soil-phys-131}}, plus its elevation above a datum, expressed as a length. It is read as the height of the water surface in a piezometer, a narrow standpipe, against a common datum. Total head adds elevation head to the head described in {{ref:soil-phys-223}}, h = ψ + z, a simplified form of the Bernoulli principle. Take a piezometer 400 m deep at 1000 m elevation, with water 100 m down: z = 600 m, ψ = 300 m and h = 900 m. Each extra meter of fresh water adds about 9.8 kPa of pressure. Where head is constant, nothing flows. A head difference drives water from higher to lower head. Since density varies with temperature and salinity, heads are first converted to fresh water head. In 1907 USDA soil physicist Edgar Buckingham showed that rising atmospheric pressure lowers well water levels.

soil-phys-198.title: Colloids, the hitchhikers that carry pollutants far
soil-phys-198.text: Plutonium at the Nevada Nuclear Test Site may have traveled far on tiny passengers. In transport facilitated by {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, these particles carry contaminants through surface water and groundwater. Radionuclides, heavy metals and organic pollutants sorb easily onto them while they are suspended. These may be inorganic, such as clays and iron oxy-hydroxides, or organic, such as humic and fulvic substances. How far they move depends on soil structure, compaction and particle size. Compacted {{ref:soil-chem-100}} and deep clay ultrafilter them. The process drew real attention only in the 1980s.

soil-phys-212.title: How much to irrigate, how much to drain
soil-phys-212.text: In the Netherlands, 720 mm of precipitation against 540 mm of evaporation gives a winter drainage requirement of 180 mm. Water balances tell how much water a field needs from irrigation and must lose through drains or wells. With surface evaporation neglected and actual evapotranspiration set to potential, the topsoil balance gives Irr = Epo + Osu + Per − Rai − Cap. Dividing Epo by Irr gives the fraction of irrigation water the crop consumes, the measure covered in {{ref:soil-agri-014}}. Drain and well discharges in the balances give the drainage requirements central to designing drainage systems. In the Dutch case, shallow-rooted pastures need summer irrigation; deep-rooted wheat practically does not.

soil-water-007.title: Coastal erosion: waves against the shore
soil-water-007.text: A wave's most effective weapon is the sediment it carries. Coastal erosion is the wearing away of shorelines, mainly by currents and waves, with changes in sea level also playing a part. Waves work by hydraulic action, pounding, corrosion of rock such as limestone by carbonic acid, and attrition of their own load. Abrasion, also covered in {{ref:soil-water-271}}, in which waves hurl sediment at cliffs, is the fastest and most effective. Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast, and erosion occurs where less arrives from upcurrent than is carried away. Sea-level rise caused by climate change has greatly increased coastal erosion rates.

soil-water-031.title: Wind abrasion: sandblasting that mattered less than thought
soil-water-031.text: Desert mushroom rocks were once blamed on blowing sand. Wind abrasion, also covered in {{ref:soil-water-271}}, is the wearing of rock and landforms by wind-driven grains. It was long thought a major cause of desert erosion, but by the mid-20th century it was judged much less important. Mushroom rocks are now credited to other processes. Wind rarely lifts sand far: most stays within 50 cm of the surface, and practically none rises above 2 m. Yardangs, rock ridges up to tens of metres high streamlined by desert winds, are widely attributed to abrasion. Polished or faceted stones called ventifacts are rare, needing abundant sand, strong winds and no vegetation.

soil-water-061.title: Mapping where the next landslide will strike
soil-water-061.text: Landslide hazard mapping rests on one assumption: future slides will happen under the same conditions as past ones. Analysts study the factors behind earlier landslides, usually grouped as {{ref:soil-water-295}}, geology, land use and land cover, and hydrogeology. Mapping software, the subject of {{ref:soil-agri-165}}, handles the many layered factors. Aerial photos and satellite images taken before and after events record where slides happened and what set them off. A good hazard map shows past events and clearly marks probable future sites, so planners can reduce losses.

soil-water-155.title: Soil moisture, the quarter of a loam that keeps plants alive
soil-water-155.text: Half of a loam's volume is solid. Gas fills a quarter and water the other quarter, and only about half of that water is available to most plants. The water held in a soil, measured by volume or by weight, is soil moisture. It shapes soil formation, structure, stability and erosion, but its main importance is for plant growth. Water makes up 80–95% of a plant's protoplasm. It carries nutrients as a solvent and keeps plants upright through turgor, the pressure of water inside their cells. Water leaves a field in four ways: as runoff across the surface, as water draining through the soil, by evaporation from the surface and by transpiration from plants. Inside the soil it moves under gravity, osmosis and capillarity. Entering water drives air out of the largest pores and can burst air-filled aggregates, a process called slaking. Roots empty the largest pores first. Water in the smallest pores clings so tightly to particles that roots cannot take it, so availability depends strongly on texture. Moving water also dissolves solutes and {{ref:soil-chem-154}} and redeposits them lower in the profile, a process called leaching. Probes such as {{ref:soil-water-225}} and {{ref:soil-water-170}} measure soil moisture in place, and remote sensing estimates it from afar.

soil-water-201.title: Darcy's law, born in the sand filters of Dijon
soil-water-201.text: From the 1830s the engineer Henry Darcy studied water flowing through sand filters, hoping to improve the water supply of Dijon, France. In 1856 he published the result in a construction report. Darcy's law is an equation describing the flow of a fluid through a porous medium, and it became the basis of {{ref:soil-phys-208}}. Like Ohm's law for electricity, it makes flow rate proportional to a difference, here in {{ref:soil-phys-165}}. Hydraulic conductivity plays the part of electrical conductivity. Flow rises with the medium's permeability, its cross-section and the pressure drop. It falls with the fluid's viscosity and the length of the path. Without a pressure gradient nothing flows. The Darcy flux is a flow per unit area, not the speed of water in the pores; porosity links the two. The law holds only for slow, smooth, laminar flow, as in most groundwater, at Reynolds numbers below one, and up to 10 in tests. Very coarse sediments may flow turbulently and escape it.

soil-water-233.title: Measuring how much of a landscape is sealed
soil-water-233.text: About 76 percent of the conterminous United States has less than 1 percent impervious cover. Total impervious area is the share of an area covered by impervious surfaces, given as a fraction from zero to one or as a percentage. It is estimated with mapping software, the subject of {{ref:soil-agri-165}}, from land-cover data, land-use categories, percent developed area or population density. The US NLCD maps it in 30-metre pixels, from 0 to 100 percent. Percentage imperviousness, or PIMP, matters in drainage and can be estimated as 6.4 times the square root of the number of dwellings per hectare. PIMP is about 10% for woodland and 100% for dense commercial areas.

soil-fert-005.title: Reading the three numbers on a fertilizer bag
soil-fert-005.text: A bag marked 10-10-10 carries three promises. The NPK rating is a label of three numbers, separated by dashes, giving a fertilizer's content of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. They are percentages of nitrogen, P2O5 and K2O. Yet the fertilizer contains no actual P2O5 or K2O; the oxides are a conventional shorthand for its phosphorus and potassium. UK rules let the elemental phosphorus and potassium values follow in parentheses, so a label can read 15-30-15 (15-13-13). Australia adds a fourth number, for sulfur, and gives elemental values for all nutrients.
